1: # MISSION.md Format
2: 
3: `MISSION.md` lives at the workspace root. It captures the _reason_ the user is learning this topic. Every teaching decision (what to teach next, which resources to surface, which exercises to design) should trace back to this document.
4: 
5: ## Template
6: 
7: ```md
8: # Mission: {Topic}
9: 
10: ## Why
11: {1-3 sentences. The concrete real-world goal the user is chasing. What changes in their life or work when they have this skill? Avoid abstract framings like "to understand X"; push for the underlying outcome.}
12: 
13: ## Success looks like
14: - {A specific, observable thing the user will be able to do}
15: - {Another specific thing}
16: - {…}
17: 
18: ## Constraints
19: - {Time, budget, prior commitments, learning preferences, anything that bounds the approach}
20: 
21: ## Out of scope
22: - {Adjacent topics the user explicitly does not want to chase right now, protecting the zone of proximal development}
23: ```
24: 
25: ## Rules
26: 
27: - **One mission per workspace.** If the user wants to learn two unrelated things, that is two workspaces.
28: - **Concrete over abstract.** "Run a half marathon by October" beats "get fitter." "Ship a Rust CLI to my team" beats "learn Rust."
29: - **Push back on vagueness.** If the user cannot articulate why, interview them before writing anything. A bad mission is worse than no mission.
30: - **Revise when reality shifts.** Missions change. When the user's goal moves, update this file: don't leave a stale mission steering future sessions.
31: - **Keep it short.** If `MISSION.md` runs past a screen, it has stopped being a compass and started being a plan.

1: # RESOURCES.md Format
2: 
3: `RESOURCES.md` is the curated set of trusted sources for this topic. Knowledge for explainers should be drawn from here, not from parametric guesses. Wisdom comes from the communities listed here.
4: 
5: ## Structure
6: 
7: ```md
8: # {Topic} Resources
9: 
10: ## Knowledge
11: 
12: - [Book: _The Science and Practice of Strength Training_ by Zatsiorsky & Kraemer](https://example.com)
13:   Foundational text on programming and adaptation. Use for: anything to do with periodisation, recovery, intensity zones.
14: - [Article: "How Much Should I Train?" by Greg Nuckols (Stronger By Science)](https://example.com)
15:   Evidence-based review of volume landmarks. Use for: weekly set targets per muscle group.
16: 
17: ## Wisdom (Communities)
18: 
19: - [r/weightroom](https://reddit.com/r/weightroom)
20:   High-signal subreddit, moderated against bro-science. Use for: programme critique, plateau troubleshooting.
21: - Local: Tuesday strength class at {gym name}
22:   Use for: real-time coaching feedback on lifts.
23: ```
24: 
25: ## Rules
26: 
27: - **High-trust only.** Prefer primary sources, recognised experts, peer-reviewed work, and communities with strong moderation. If a resource is marketing dressed as education, leave it out.
28: - **Annotate every entry.** A bare link is useless in three months. Add one line: what it covers and when to reach for it.
29: - **Group by Knowledge / Wisdom.** Mirrors the philosophy in [SKILL.md](./SKILL.md). It is fine for a resource to appear in only one group.
30: - **Surface gaps explicitly.** If no good resource exists for an area the mission needs, write a `## Gaps` section listing what is missing. This drives future search.
31: - **Prune ruthlessly.** A resource that turned out to be wrong, shallow, or off-mission should be removed, not buried. Better five sharp sources than thirty mediocre ones.
32: - **Record community preferences.** If the user has opted out of joining communities, note it here so future sessions don't keep proposing them.

1: # Learning Record Format
2: 
3: Learning records live in `./learning-records/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc. Create the directory lazily: only when the first record is written.
4: 
5: They are the teaching equivalent of ADRs: they capture non-obvious lessons, key insights, and stated prior knowledge that will steer future sessions. They are used to calculate the zone of proximal development.
6: 
7: ## Template
8: 
9: ```md
10: # {Short title of what was learned or established}
11: 
12: {1-3 sentences: what was learned (or what prior knowledge was established), and why it matters for future sessions.}
13: ```
14: 
15: That is the whole format. A learning record can be a single paragraph. The value is recording _that_ this is now known and _why_ it changes what to teach next, not in filling out sections.
16: 
17: ## Optional sections
18: 
19: Only include these when they add genuine value. Most records won't need them.
20: 
21: - **Status** frontmatter (`active | superseded by LR-NNNN`): useful when an earlier understanding turns out to be wrong and is replaced.
22: - **Evidence**: how the user demonstrated the understanding (a question answered, an exercise completed, prior experience cited). Useful when the claim might be revisited.
23: - **Implications**: what this unlocks or rules out for future sessions. Worth recording when non-obvious.
24: 
25: ## Numbering
26: 
27: Scan `./learning-records/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.
28: 
29: ## When to write a learning record
30: 
31: Write one when any of these is true:
32: 
33: 1. **The user demonstrated genuine understanding of something non-trivial**: not just exposure, but evidence they can use the concept correctly. This sets a new floor for what to teach next.
34: 2. **The user disclosed prior knowledge**: "I already know X." Record it so future sessions don't re-teach it. Also record the _depth_ claimed.
35: 3. **A misconception was corrected**: the user previously believed something wrong and now sees why. These are high-value: they predict future stumbling blocks for related topics.
36: 4. **The mission shifted in response to learning**: the user discovered they cared about something different than they thought. Cross-link to [[MISSION.md]] and update it.
37: 
38: ### What does _not_ qualify
39: 
40: - Material that was merely covered. Coverage is not learning. Wait for evidence.
41: - Anything already captured tersely in [[GLOSSARY.md]] as a term definition. Don't duplicate.
42: - Session-by-session activity logs. Learning records are not a journal: they are decision-grade insights.
43: 
44: ## Supersession
45: 
46: When a later record contradicts an earlier one (the user's understanding deepened or corrected), mark the old record `Status: superseded by LR-NNNN` rather than deleting it. The history of how understanding evolved is itself useful signal.

1: # GLOSSARY.md Format
2: 
3: `GLOSSARY.md` is the canonical language for this teaching workspace. All explainers, exercises, and learning records should adhere to its terminology. Building it is itself part of learning: compressing a concept into a tight definition is evidence the user understands it.
4: 
5: ## Structure
6: 
7: ```md
8: # {Topic} Glossary
9: 
10: {One or two sentence description of the topic this glossary covers.}
11: 
12: ## Terms
13: 
14: **Hypertrophy**:
15: Muscle growth driven by mechanical tension and metabolic stress over repeated training sessions.
16: _Avoid_: Bulking, getting big
17: 
18: **Progressive overload**:
19: Systematically increasing the demand on a muscle over time, via load, volume, or intensity.
20: _Avoid_: Pushing harder, levelling up
21: 
22: **RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion)**:
23: A 1–10 self-rating of how hard a set felt, where 10 is failure and 8 means two reps left in the tank.
24: _Avoid_: Effort score, intensity rating
25: ```
26: 
27: ## Rules
28: 
29: - **Add a term only when the user understands it.** The glossary is a record of compressed knowledge, not a dictionary the user reads to learn. If the user has just been introduced to a concept, wait until they can use it correctly before promoting it here.
30: - **Be opinionated.** When several words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the rest as aliases to avoid. This is how language compresses.
31: - **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences. Define what the term IS, not what it does or how to do it.
32: - **Use the glossary's own terms inside definitions.** Once a term is in the glossary, prefer it everywhere, including inside other definitions. This is what makes complex terms easier to grasp later.
33: - **Group under subheadings** when natural clusters emerge (e.g. `## Anatomy`, `## Programming`). A flat list is fine when terms cohere.
34: - **Flag ambiguities explicitly.** If a term is used loosely in the wider field, note the resolution: "In this workspace, 'set' always means a working set; warm-ups are tracked separately."
35: - **Revise as understanding deepens.** A definition the user wrote in week one may be wrong by week six. Update in place; do not leave stale entries.

The search for ""are we game yet" rust gamedev roadmap learning resources" returned the following summary:
Diving into Rust game development requires a "bring-your-own-glue" mindset[1][2], but the ecosystem has matured significantly. 

The essential roadmap, core hubs like **"Are We Game Yet?"**, and top-tier learning resources provide a clear path forward for Rust gamedev:

---

### 1. The Central Hub: "Are We Game Yet?"
* **Website:** [arewegameyet.rs](https://arewegameyet.rs/)[3]
* **What it is:** The community-driven registry tracking the state of Rust game development. 
* **Why use it:** Instead of guessing which libraries are production-ready, this site categorizes active crates for **Engines, Rendering, Audio, Physics, UI, Asset Management, and Mathematics**. 

---

### 2. The Rust Gamedev Roadmap
If you are mapping out how to go from absolute beginner to making games in Rust, follow this structured path:

#### Step 1: Learn Core Rust
You cannot skip learning Rust's strict memory model. Focus heavily on ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, and structs/enums[4].
* **The Rust Book** (*The Book*): The official, mandatory starting point[3][5].
* **Rust by Example**: Practical, runnable snippets of core concepts[3].

#### Step 2: Pick Your Approach (Engine vs. Framework vs. From Scratch)
Rust gamedev generally splits into three paths:
* **The Full Engine Approach (Most Popular/Usable):** Use **Bevy**[1]—a data-driven game engine built entirely around an Entity Component System (ECS). It is fast, modular, and heavily supported.
* **The Lightweight Framework Approach:** Use libraries like **Macroquad** (great for 2D/quick prototypes)[3] or **ggez**.
* **The Low-Level / Modular Approach:** Build your own structure using **wgpu** (Rust's safe, portable implementation of WebGPU) for rendering and **winit** for windowing[1].

---

### 3. Essential Learning Resources & Books

#### 📚 Hands-On Books & Tutorials
* ***Hands-On Rust: Effective L
<truncated 836 bytes>
y tracking the Bevy game engine ecosystem[6].
* **Rust GameDev Working Group:** The official community hub hosting discussions, matrix/Discord channels, and collaborative projects[6].

### Suggested First Project
If you want a tried-and-true entry point: 
1. Finish the first few chapters of **The Rust Book**[5].
2. Open up **Bevy's official quick-start guide** and try to spawn a 3D cube or 2D sprite on screen[1]. 
3. Recreate a classic clone like **Pong, Snake, or Tetris**[1] to understand how game loops, inputs, and state management work in Rust's ownership paradigm.

To get started with the **Bevy Game Engine** (a data-driven game engine built in Rust using an Entity Component System architecture)[1][2], you can utilize its official documentation and learning guides[3].

### 1. Official Documentation & Tutorials
* **Official Website & Learning Hub:** [bevyengine.org](https://bevyengine.org/)[4]
* **The Quick Start Guide / Bevy Book:** The official interactive guide takes you through setting up your environment, understanding the ECS paradigm (Entities, Components, Systems), and building small projects like a clone of *Breakout* or a *Falling Sand* simulation[3][5][6].
* **API Documentation:** [Bevy API Docs](https://docs.rs/bevy/) provides comprehensive reference documentation for all types, traits, and methods[4].
* **Official Examples:** The [Bevy GitHub Repository Examples Folder](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/tree/main/examples) contains hundreds of isolated, runnable examples showcasing 2D/3D rendering, audio, input handling, UI, and physics.

---

### 2. Quick Start: Your First Bevy Project

#### Step A: Install Prerequisites
Bevy requires a working **Rust toolchain** (latest stable release recommended)[7][5]. Make sure Rust is installed via [rustup.rs](https://www.rust-up.rs/). 

Depending on your operating system, you may also need to install system dependencies (like audio or windowing development libraries)[7]. Check the official [Bevy Setup OS Dependencies Documentation](https://bevyengine.org/learn/) for platform-specific requirements (such as Linux `udev` or graphics drivers).

#### Step B: Create a New Rust Project
Open your terminal and run[7]:
```bash
cargo new my_bevy_game
cd my_bevy_game
```

#### Step C: Add Bevy as a Dependency
You can add Bevy to your `Cargo.toml` using `cargo add`[7]:
```bash
cargo add bevy
```
*(Alternatively, manually add `bevy = "0.19"`—or whichever c

***Hands-on Rust: Effective Learning through 2D Game Development and Play*** is a programming book written by **Herbert Wolverson** and published by **The Pragmatic Bookshelf**[1][2]. 

### Overview
The book is designed to teach the Rust programming language through a practical, project-based approach rather than traditional abstract syntax tutorials[1][2]. By focusing on game development, it introduces core language concepts—such as ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, structs, enums, and pattern matching—while building playable 2D games from scratch[1][2].

### Key Projects Covered
1. **Flappy Lizard (A Flappy Bird Clone):** Used early in the book to help readers get comfortable with basic syntax, control flow, functions, and setting up a development environment[2].
2. **Dungeon Crawler:** A full rogue-like game built over the majority of the book. This project introduces more advanced topics like:
   * Random procedural dungeon generation[2]
   * Managing game state and entities
   * Implementing component-based architectures 
   * Handling user input and rendering with `bracket-lib` (a minimalist ASCII/console game engine created by the author)[3]
   * Managing concurrency and performance optimization[2]

### What You Learn
* **Core Rust Philosophy:** Understanding memory safety[2] without a garbage collector through Rust's unique ownership model.
* **Idiomatic Code:** How to structure medium-sized Rust applications cleanly.
* **Minimalist Game Design:** Creating engaging mechanics using constraints (such as ASCII graphics) before getting bogged down in complex asset pipelines[3].

***

*(Note: Herbert Wolverson also authored a follow-up book with The Pragmatic Bookshelf titled **Advanced Hands-on Rust: Level Up Your Coding Skills**, which targets higher-level concepts like macros, traits, asynchronous programming, and working with the Bevy game engine[4].)*

"# Game Development in Rust Resources

## Knowledge

- [The Rust Programming Language ("The Book") by Steve Klabnik & Carol Nichols](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/)
  The canonical Rust guide. Use for: core syntax, ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, traits, and error handling before touching complex game architectures.
- [Are We Game Yet? Ecosystem Catalog](https://arewegameyet.rs/)
  Community-maintained registry of Rust game dev crates. Use for: finding vetted crates for math, windowing, audio, physics, and rendering.
- [Hands-on Rust by Herbert Wolverson (Pragmatic Bookshelf)](https://pragprog.com/titles/hwrust/hands-on-rust/)
  Practical, 2D game-first introduction to Rust. Use for: learning Rust syntax and data structures through concrete playable games (Flappy Bird clone, Dungeon Crawler).
- [Bevy Official Documentation & Examples](https://bevyengine.org/learn/)
  The primary hub for Rust's most popular ECS game engine. Use for: learning modern Entity Component System architecture, 2D/3D pipelines, asset management, and schedule systems.
- [Macroquad Documentation & Guide](https://macroquad.rs/)
  Minimalist, immediate-style 2D framework heavily inspired by Raylib. Use for: rapid game prototyping, 2D arcade games, game jams, and mastering game loops without framework overhead.
- [Learn WGPU by Sotrh (Benjamin Hansen)](https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/)
  Complete step-by-step guide to modern graphics in Rust. Use for: learning graphics pipelines, WGSL shaders, buffers, and building custom renderers from scratch.
- [Rust Roguelike Tutorial by Herbert Wolverson](https://bfnightly.bracketproductions.com/)
  Comprehensive classic tutorial. Use for: turn-based game loops, field-of-view algorithms, procedural generation, and component-based entity management.

## Wisdom (Communities)

- [Rust GameDev Discord & Monthly Newsletter](https://discord.gg/rust-gamedev)
  Central hub for the Rust GameDev Working Group. Use for: troubleshooting niche ecosystem crates, getting project feedback, and
<truncated 423 bytes>

"# Teaching Notes & Preferences

- **Host Environment**: NixOS 26.11 (Zokor). Native builds of graphics/audio crates (Bevy, Macroquad, WGPU) will require a `shell.nix` or `flake.nix` with system libraries (Vulkan, Wayland/X11, ALSA, libxkbcommon, udev).
- **Starting Point**: Learning game dev in Rust from zero.
- **Pending Questions**:
  - What prior programming experience does the user have (complete beginner to code vs experienced programmer new to Rust)?
  - What target game genre / milestone do they want to build (2D arcade/roguelike, Bevy ECS, or custom engine from scratch)?
